name: Barcelona El Prat
brief: Three runways in two directions that cross each other, and a great deal of traffic. The parallels take the arrivals while the crosswind runway is worked around them, so the two flows are dependent -- what you do with one constrains the other, and the intersection is a place two aircraft must never be at once. Arrivals come from Europe to the north, north Africa to the south and the Atlantic to the west, and the Mediterranean transit lanes run straight across the arrival streams at levels the arrivals are descending through. Add a noise abatement floor over the coast and the city that takes away the low airspace where you would otherwise turn traffic in, and there is very little room left to be untidy in.

provenance.notes: The aerodrome reference point, the runway designators and bearings, and the field elevation are real to the best of the author knowledge. EVERYTHING ELSE IS CONSTRUCTED: the entry fixes and their names, the airspace boundary, the terrain and noise areas and the traffic mix are invented to give the sector a shape to control, and are NOT taken from any AIP. Do not use for anything but this game. Contrast egll.json, whose positions are surveyed. Runway thresholds are derived from the strip: a centre on the reference point, the published bearing, and the published length, with the two ends half a length either side. Only the aerodrome VOR carries a frequency; the entry gates are plain waypoints. Terrain is drawn as nested contour bands, each the ground above a height, with the summits at their real positions and heights; the outlines between them are shaped by hand to sit right against the coast and are not surveyed. The airspace volumes are CONSTRUCTED and are not from any AIP or sector file: a control zone shaped round the runway, approach corridors on the extended centrelines, and terminal sectors whose floors step up away from the arrival direction and over the high ground in this file. They carry derivation "approx". Aerodrome traffic zones are computed from a rule -- 2.5 NM where the longest runway is over 1850 m and 2 NM otherwise, to 2000 ft above the aerodrome -- and carry derivation "rule". The control zone and the terminal area outline are unchanged and still rule-derived. Everything else in the airspace block is CONSTRUCTED and comes from no AIP or sector file: approach corridors along the extended centrelines, which bring the base of controlled airspace down to 1500 ft outside the zone, and terminal sub-areas whose bases step up away from the arrival direction and over the high ground in this file. They carry derivation "approx". None of them encloses the aerodrome, so none of them joins the area of responsibility: that is still the control zone and the terminal area, exactly as before. Aerodrome traffic zones are computed from a rule -- 2.5 NM where the longest runway is over 1850 m and 2 NM otherwise, to 2000 ft above the aerodrome -- and carry derivation "rule".

challenge: Crossing runways, four gates, noise floors and transits through the arrivals.
